scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

prediction.raw: **0 (Not AAITA)** **Here's why, step by step:** ### ✅ **You did nothing technically wrong** - **No assigned seating**: You explicitly confirmed there are no reserved seats ( "All seats are first come, first served"). - **Not a priority seat**: You were in a *regular* front-row seat, **not** one of the two designated "priority seats" for disabled students. Those are the * only* seats legally reserved for registered accommodations. - **No disability documentation required for you**: Your anxiety is a valid reason for needing front-row seating (many students have similar needs), but ** you don’t need to "register" to sit there**. The school’s policy only requires registration for *priority* seats. ### ⚠️ **Girl 1’s claims don’t hold up** - **"I need a front seat because I’m hard of hearing"**: - If she *truly* needed a disability accommodation, **she would have registered with the disability services office**. Universities *require* formal documentation to reserve priority seating. - **Her hearing aid alone is not proof of a documented accommodation**. Many people use hearing aids without formal disability status (e.g., mild hearing loss). - **"It’s my seat"**: - This is a **social myth**, not a rule. Classmates often *feel* entitled to seats they’ve occupied before, but **"my seat" doesn’t exist in a first-c come, first-served system**. - **Her behavior was aggressive and inappropriate** ( "Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus"). You had no obligation to comply with demands that violated school policy. ### 🔍 **Key red flags in her story** - **She chose the * far left corner* seat** ( "10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in"). - If she * genuinely* needed front-row seating for hearing, ** she would have chosen a center seat** (closer to the professor’s voice and whiteboard). - This strongly suggests ** her " hearing need" was a pretext** to claim a seat * next to Girl 2* for worksheet collaboration (as you suspected). - **"I don’t need to register or explain myself"**: - **This is the opposite of how disability accommodations work**. If she * had* a documented need, she * would* need to register and * would* need to explain it to the school ( not to you). - Her refusal to engage with the process reveals her claim was likely fabricated. ### 💡 **How you * could* have handled it better (but it’s not your fault)** - **Empathy first**: " I didn realize you needed this seat for hearing— let me check if there’s a priority seat available for you." - **Redirect to the right authority**: " I’m not sure about accommodations, but you should talk to the disability services office or professor about priority seating if you need it." - **But crucially**: **You were not obligated to do any of this**. Her aggressive tone and false claims made de-escalation unnecessary. ### 🌟 **Final verdict** - **You did nothing wrong**. You followed the rules, didn’t occupy a reserved seat, and had no duty to surrender your spot to someone making unverified claims. - **Girl 1 and Girl 2 were in the wrong** for: - Misrepresenting disability needs ( no documentation, no formal request to the school), - Using aggression to enforce a " social norm" that doesn’t exist, - Prioritizing worksheet collaboration over genuine accommodation. - **The "talking shit" behind you** is on them—not you. They’re the ones who broke classroom etiquette by being hostile over a non-issue. **You’re not AITA.** Sit where you need to sit. If someone else has a * documented* disability accommodation, * they* should handle it with the school—not confront you. *P.S. Next time, if you’re anxious about front-row seating, consider a quick email to the professor: " I have anxiety that makes it hard to participate from the back— is it okay if I consistently sit in the front row?" (Most professors will say yes, no questions asked).* 😊
